eagle-and-jaguar-warriors.s: The Eagle and Jaguar warriors were elite military orders of the Aztec Empire. Membership was earned mainly by capturing enemies in battle, and it brought high status, distinctive costumes and privileges.

early-dynastic-period.s: The Early Dynastic period is the phase of southern Mesopotamian history, roughly the first half of the third millennium BCE, when Sumerian city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash and Kish competed for dominance. It preceded the unification of Mesopotamia by Sargon and the rise of…

early-muslim-conquests.s: The early Muslim conquests were the rapid expansion of the Arab Muslim state in the 7th century, following the death of the Prophet Muhammad. Arab armies overran the Sasanian Empire and took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium, and expansion continued under the Umayyad Caliphate.

east-africa.s: East Africa is the eastern region of the African continent, including the Horn of Africa and the Swahili coast. It was home to the Aksumite Empire and a target of colonial expansion by the Portuguese Empire, the German Empire and the Italian Empire.

east-african-campaign-world-war-ii.s: The East African campaign was a Second World War campaign fought in 1940–1941 between British and Commonwealth forces, with Ethiopian resistance fighters, and the Italian forces in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Italian Somaliland. Its outcome destroyed Italian East Africa, restored…

east-francia.s: East Francia was the eastern kingdom created when the Carolingian Empire was divided by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, initially under Louis the German. Covering much of present-day Germany, it developed into the Kingdom of Germany and became the core of the later Holy Roman…

east-india-company.s: The East India Company was an English, later British, chartered trading company founded in 1600. Beginning as a trading concern, it became a military and governing power in India, defeating the Maratha Empire and the Sikh Empire and reducing the Mughal Empire to a pensioner,…

east-indies.s: The East Indies is a historical term for the islands of South-East Asia, especially the Indonesian archipelago. The Dutch East Indies formed the centre of the Dutch Empire, valued for spices and later plantation crops, until the Empire of Japan occupied them during the Second…

east-timor.s: East Timor (Timor-Leste) is a country occupying the eastern half of the island of Timor in South-East Asia. It was a Portuguese colony for centuries and one of the last remnants of the Portuguese Empire; after Portugal withdrew in 1975 it was occupied by Indonesia and became…

eastern-europe.s: Eastern Europe is the eastern part of the European continent, including the plains between the Baltic, the Black Sea and the Urals. The Khazar Khaganate dominated much of its south-eastern steppe and trade routes, while the Mongol Empire conquered the Rus' principalities and…

eastern-orthodox-church.s: The Eastern Orthodox Church is the body of Christian churches that follow the Byzantine tradition and recognise the authority of the ecumenical councils, separating from Rome in the Middle Ages. It was the state church of the Byzantine Empire and later of the Russian Empire,…

eastern-turkestan.s: Eastern Turkestan is a historical name for the Tarim Basin and surrounding lands, roughly corresponding to southern Xinjiang in north-western China. The Qing Empire conquered the region in the eighteenth century after defeating the Dzungars, and it later reasserted control…

eastern-turkic-khaganate.s: The Eastern Turkic Khaganate was the eastern half of the Gokturk realm after it split into eastern and western branches in the late sixth century. Based in Mongolia, it was a major power on China's northern frontier until the Tang Dynasty under Emperor Taizong defeated it in…

ebarat-ii.s: Ebarat II was an Elamite ruler of around 1900 BCE. According to the site's account, he established the sukkalmah system, a tripartite governing hierarchy that is regarded as the most sophisticated constitutional innovation of the Elamite Confederation.

ebla.s: Ebla was an ancient city in northern Syria that flourished in the third millennium BCE and is famous for its large archive of cuneiform tablets. It fell to the Akkadian Empire during the campaigns of Sargon or Naram-Sin, whose conquests extended Akkadian reach to its greatest…

ebony.s: Ebony is a dense, dark hardwood from tropical Africa that was highly valued as a luxury material in the ancient world. It was among the goods that moved from the African interior to Egypt, appearing in the trade of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, including Hatshepsut's…

ebro-river.s: The Ebro is a major river of north-eastern Spain, flowing into the Mediterranean. At its height the Almoravid Empire stretched from the Senegal River in West Africa to the Ebro, marking the northern limit of its territory in al-Andalus.

ecbatana.s: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in western Iran, was the capital of the Median Empire. After Cyrus the Great conquered Media, it became one of the royal residences and administrative centres of the Achaemenid Empire, used especially as a summer capital.

ecological-warfare.s: Ecological warfare refers to military methods that target an enemy's environment and resources, such as water supplies or farmland. Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire is credited with this approach, destroying Eshnunna around 1755 BCE by damming its water supply instead of…

edict-of-milan.s: The Edict of Milan was the agreement of 313 CE between the emperors Constantine and Licinius granting religious toleration throughout the Roman Empire, including to Christians. It ended official persecution and opened the way to the rise of Christianity as the empire's…

edict-of-telipinu.s: The Edict of Telipinu is a Hittite text issued by King Telipinu around 1525 BCE. It recounts earlier periods of royal murder and instability and establishes rules of succession to the throne, along with procedures for punishing crimes within the royal family.

edicts-of-ashoka.s: The Edicts of Ashoka are a series of inscriptions on rocks and pillars issued by the Maurya emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE. They proclaim his commitment to dharma, his remorse after the Kalinga war, and policies of tolerance, welfare and moral government.

edirne.s: Edirne, the ancient Adrianople, is a city in European Turkey near the Greek and Bulgarian borders. It served as the capital of the Ottoman Empire before the conquest of Constantinople in 1453, and it is home to the Selimiye Mosque, regarded as a masterpiece of the architect…

edo-tokyo.s: Edo, renamed Tokyo in 1868, was the seat of the Tokugawa Shogunate. Tokugawa Ieyasu made it his base, and it grew into one of the largest cities in the world, partly because the alternate attendance system required daimyo to spend time there.

edo-bay.s: Edo Bay, now Tokyo Bay, is the bay on which Edo stands. In 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry's 'Black Ships' entered it and demanded that Japan open to American trade, exposing the military weakness of the Tokugawa Shogunate and setting in motion the events that led to its fall.

edo-people.s: The Edo people, also called the Bini, are an ethnic group of southern Nigeria. They founded and formed the core population of the Benin Empire, whose capital, Benin City, and Oba institution remain central to Edo identity, along with the celebrated Benin bronzes.

edo-period.s: The Edo period is the era of Japanese history from 1603 to 1868 under the rule of the Tokugawa Shogunate, named after its capital Edo. It was a long period of internal peace, restricted foreign contact, urban growth and cultural flourishing, during which the samurai became…

edward-ullendorff.s: Edward Ullendorff was a British scholar of Semitic languages and Ethiopian studies. The Ethiopian Empire profile cites his judgement that Emperor Zara Yaqob was the greatest Ethiopian ruler since the Aksumite era.

egon-schiele.s: Egon Schiele was an Austrian expressionist painter active in Vienna in the early twentieth century, known for his intense figure drawings and portraits. He is cited, alongside Klimt and Kokoschka, as part of the cultural flowering of Vienna in the late Austro-Hungarian Empire.

egypt.s: Egypt is a country in north-eastern Africa centred on the Nile valley, one of the oldest centres of civilisation. Its wealth and position made it a prize for many empires: it was the core of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and the Ptolemaic Empire, and was ruled by the…

egyptian-conquest-of-kordofan.s: The Egyptian conquest of Kordofan in 1821 was part of the expansion of Muhammad Ali's Egypt into Sudan. It removed Kordofan from the Darfur Sultanate, severing its eastern trade connections and diverting Nile valley commerce, which led to a long economic decline that weakened…

egyptian-hieroglyphs.s: Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, using pictorial signs for sounds and words. The peace treaty between the Hittite Empire and Egypt after Kadesh survives both in Akkadian cuneiform at Hattusa and in hieroglyphs at Karnak, illustrating the…

egyptians.s: The Egyptians are the people of the Nile valley in north-eastern Africa. In antiquity they formed the population of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, served as soldiers and subjects under the Achaemenid Empire, and under the Ptolemaic Empire were recruited into the army,…

ehengbuda.s: Ehengbuda was an Oba of Benin who died in 1606. He is regarded as the last of the great warrior kings who, from Ewuare onward, combined military expansion with artistic patronage.

eight-banners.s: The Eight Banners were the military and administrative organisation created by the Manchu leader Nurhaci around 1601. All Manchu households were enrolled in banners, later joined by Mongol and Han banners.

eighteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Eighteenth Dynasty was the ruling house of Egypt that founded the New Kingdom after the expulsion of the Hyksos. Its rulers, including Ahmose I, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten and Tutankhamun, built the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, extending Egyptian power into the…

einhard.s: Einhard was a Frankish scholar and courtier at the court of Charlemagne. He wrote the Life of Charlemagne, a biography that is one of the most important sources for the reign of the emperor and for the government of the Carolingian Empire.

ejisu.s: Ejisu is a town in the Ashanti region of present-day Ghana. Its queen mother, Yaa Asantewaa, led the War of the Golden Stool against the British in 1900, the last major armed resistance of the Ashanti Empire against colonial rule.

el-fasher.s: El Fasher is a city in western Sudan that became the capital of the Darfur Sultanate. From there the sultan governed through a hierarchy of territorial title-holders, and the city was again the seat of the restored sultanate under Ali Dinar.

el-hadj-umar-tall.s: El Hadj Umar Tall was a West African Muslim scholar and military leader of the nineteenth century who founded the Toucouleur state through conquests in the 1850s and 1860s. The Sokoto Caliphate profile identifies him among the jihad leaders who drew inspiration from Sokoto's…

elam.s: Elam was an ancient region in south-western Iran, centred on Susa and the highlands of Anshan. Its rulers were long-standing rivals of Mesopotamian states, clashing with the Akkadian Empire, the Babylonian Empire and the Assyrian Empire.

elamite-confederation.s: The Elamite Confederation refers to the states of ancient Elam in south-western Iran, which endured for more than two thousand years. Elam fought repeatedly with Mesopotamian powers, sacking Ur and ending the Neo-Sumerian Empire, conquering Babylon around 1158 BCE, and finally…

elamite-conquest-of-babylon-c-1158-bce.s: The Elamite conquest of Babylon around 1158 BCE was a campaign by Elamite kings, notably Shutruk-Nahhunte and his successors, which brought an end to the Kassite dynasty. The Elamites carried off monuments to Susa, including the Code of Hammurabi stele, and the episode marked…

elamite-language.s: Elamite is the extinct language of ancient Elam, written first in its own scripts and later in cuneiform. It has no known relatives.

elamite-sack-of-ur.s: The Elamite sack of Ur took place around 2004 BCE, when Elamite forces captured the city of Ur and took its last king, Ibbi-Sin, captive. It brought an end to the Neo-Sumerian Empire and was later lamented in Sumerian literature.

elamites.s: The Elamites were the people of ancient Elam in south-western Iran, who formed the Elamite Confederation. They were long-term rivals and neighbours of Mesopotamian states, contributing to the fall of the Neo-Sumerian Empire and fighting the Assyrian Empire.

elective-monarchy.s: An elective monarchy is a system in which the monarch is chosen by election rather than inheriting the throne. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth the whole nobility could take part in electing the king, who had to accept conditions limiting his powers.

el-ghaba.s: El-Ghaba was the royal town of Koumbi Saleh, the capital of the Ghana Empire. Described by Arab writers, it contained the king's stone-walled palace and a sacred grove, and stood some distance from the separate Muslim merchants' town.

elmina.s: Elmina is a town on the coast of present-day Ghana, site of São Jorge da Mina, the castle built by the Portuguese in 1482. Later taken by the Dutch, it was a major centre of the gold and slave trades, and its trade relations, including the Dutch connection, mattered to the…

emancipation-reform-of-1861.s: The emancipation reform of 1861 was the decree of Tsar Alexander II abolishing serfdom in the Russian Empire. It freed millions of peasants, though they had to pay redemption for land, and it opened a period of wider reforms in local government, the courts and the army.

emir.s: An emir is an Arabic title meaning commander or prince, used for military leaders, governors and rulers in Islamic states. In the Mamluk Sultanate emirs were the senior military officers, in the Ilkhanate powerful emirs dominated late politics, and in the Sokoto Caliphate…

emirate.s: An emirate is a territory ruled by an emir. Under the Abbasid Caliphate many provinces became effectively autonomous emirates, and the Umayyad survivors in Spain founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

emirate-of-cordoba.s: The Emirate of Córdoba was the Muslim state in Iberia founded in 756 by Abd al-Rahman I, a survivor of the Umayyad dynasty after its overthrow by the Abbasids. It preserved Umayyad rule in al-Andalus and was proclaimed a caliphate in 929, continuing the legacy of the Umayyad…

emperor-gaozu-of-tang.s: Emperor Gaozu, born Li Yuan, was the founder of the Tang Dynasty. A Sui general, he rebelled during the collapse of the Sui and founded the dynasty in 618 CE.

emperor-huizong.s: Emperor Huizong was a Northern Song emperor, celebrated as a painter, calligrapher and patron of the arts but criticised for political neglect. When the Jurchen Jin captured Kaifeng in 1127, he and his son were taken captive, ending the Northern Song and forcing the Song…

emperor-meiji.s: Emperor Meiji was emperor of Japan from 1867 to 1912. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa Shogunate and restored imperial rule in his name, and his reign saw rapid modernisation, industrialisation and the building of the Empire of Japan into a major power.

emperor-shenzong-of-song.s: Emperor Shenzong was an emperor of the Northern Song in the late eleventh century. He backed the reforms of Wang Anshi, the New Policies, which aimed to strengthen state finances and the military of the Song Dynasty but provoked intense factional opposition.

emperor-taizong-of-song.s: Emperor Taizong was the second emperor of the Song Dynasty, succeeding his brother Taizu. He completed the reunification of China by conquering the remaining southern states and Northern Han, but his campaigns against the Liao failed to recover the northern frontier regions.

emperor-taizong-of-tang.s: Emperor Taizong, born Li Shimin, was the second emperor of the Tang Dynasty (r. 626–649).

emperor-taizu-of-song.s: Emperor Taizu, born Zhao Kuangyin, was the founder of the Song Dynasty. A military commander, he seized power in 960 and began reunifying China.

emperor-wu-of-han.s: Emperor Wu was the seventh emperor of the Han Dynasty (r. 141–87 BCE).

emperor-xuanzong-of-tang.s: Emperor Xuanzong was an emperor of the Tang Dynasty (r. 713–741) whose era is remembered as a cultural and political high point.

emperor-yang-of-sui.s: Emperor Yang was the second emperor of the Sui dynasty. He undertook vast projects, including the completion of the Grand Canal, and launched costly failed campaigns against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo.

empire-of-japan.s: The Empire of Japan was the Japanese state from the Meiji Restoration of 1868 until the post-war constitution of 1947. It modernised rapidly, defeated China and Russia, acquired colonies including Taiwan and Korea, and expanded across East and South-East Asia before its defeat…

empire-on-which-the-sun-never-sets.n: Empire on which the sun never sets
empire-on-which-the-sun-never-sets.s: The 'empire on which the sun never sets' is a phrase describing an empire so extensive that some part of it is always in daylight. It was first applied to the Spanish Empire under the Habsburgs, especially after the union with Portugal in 1580, when its possessions spanned…

empress-dowager-cixi.s: Empress Dowager Cixi was the dominant figure at the Qing court from the 1860s until her death in 1908, ruling as regent for the Tongzhi and Guangxu emperors. She supported some limited modernisation but suppressed the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 and backed the Boxers in 1900.

encomienda.s: The encomienda was a system in the Spanish Empire by which the crown granted colonists the right to extract labour and tribute from groups of indigenous people, in return for protecting them and instructing them in Christianity. In practice it led to severe abuse, prompting…

end-of-kanem-bornu-independence.s: The end of Kanem–Bornu independence came in 1893, when the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered Bornu. His rule was short-lived, as the region was soon divided among the British, French and Germans, bringing to a close the long history of the Kanem-Bornu Empire as an…

endubis.s: Endubis was a king of Aksum who reigned around 270 CE. He is the first Aksumite ruler known to have issued coins, in gold, silver and bronze, making the Aksumite Empire one of the first African states outside Roman control to mint its own currency.

england.s: England is a country in the south of Great Britain. A rising maritime and commercial power from the sixteenth century, it united with Scotland in 1707 to form Great Britain and became the core of the British Empire.

english-language.s: English is a Germanic language that originated in England. Spread across the world by the British Empire through settlement, administration, education and trade, it became the language of government and elites in many colonies and is now one of the most widely spoken…

enheduanna.s: Enheduanna was the daughter of Sargon of Akkad, appointed high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She is known as the author of hymns to the goddess Inanna and is often called the first named author in history.

enmebaragesi.s: Enmebaragesi was a king of Kish who lived around 2700 BCE and is one of the earliest Mesopotamian rulers attested in inscriptions. The Sumerian King List records that he defeated the Elamites, among the earliest recorded conflicts in the history of the Elamite Confederation.

ensi.s: Ensi was a Sumerian title for the ruler or governor of a city-state. Under the Akkadian Empire, the ensis of conquered cities were brought under royal control and often replaced by loyal Akkadian appointees, turning them into provincial governors within a centralised empire.

entrepot.s: An entrepôt is a port or trading centre where goods are imported, stored and re-exported, often without further processing. Control of such hubs gave states wealth and influence; examples include Adulis for the Aksumite Empire, Zeila for the Adal Sultanate, Palembang and the…

environmental-degradation.s: Environmental degradation refers to the long-term damage of land, soil, water and forests through overuse, salinisation or deforestation, often combined with climatic change. It undermined the economic base of several states, including salinisation of fields in the…

ephor.s: Ephor was the title of senior magistrates, best known from Sparta, who supervised the conduct of kings and officials. Greek writers, notably Aristotle, compared certain Carthaginian institutions to the Spartan ephors when describing the constitution of the Punic Empire.

epic-of-gilgamesh.s: The Epic of Gilgamesh is an ancient Mesopotamian poem about the legendary king of Uruk and his search for immortality. It is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

epidemic-disease.s: Epidemic disease refers to outbreaks of infectious illness that killed large parts of a population, disrupting economies, armies and government. The Black Death struck the Mamluk Sultanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan Dynasty, while smallpox and other diseases introduced by…

equal-field-system.s: The equal-field system was a land allocation system used in China from the Northern Wei to the Tang Dynasty. The state allocated land to households according to their size and labour, linking land to tax and labour obligations.

equites.s: The equites, or equestrian order, were the second rank of the Roman aristocracy below the senators. Originally Rome's cavalry, they became a wealthy class of businessmen and, under the Roman Empire, filled important administrative posts such as prefect of Egypt.

erekle-ii.s: Erekle II was a Georgian king of the eighteenth century who served in Nader Shah's campaigns. After Nader's assassination in 1747 and the collapse of the Afsharid Empire, he asserted Georgian independence, later uniting eastern Georgia and placing it under Russian protection…

eresoyen.s: Eresoyen was an Oba of Benin in the first half of the eighteenth century. Following the near-collapse of the monarchy in the Ewuakpe civil war, his reign, along with that of Akenzua I, brought a partial recovery that stabilised the core territories of the Benin Empire.

eritrea.s: Eritrea is a country in the Horn of Africa on the Red Sea coast. The Aksumite Empire's port of Adulis lay there, and from the late nineteenth century it became Italy's first colony and a base for the Italian Empire's invasion of Ethiopia.

esagila.s: The Esagila was the great temple of Marduk in Babylon, the most important sanctuary of the city. The rulers of the Chaldean Empire, especially Nebuchadnezzar II, lavishly restored it, together with the nearby ziggurat Etemenanki, as part of their rebuilding of Babylon.

esarhaddon.s: Esarhaddon was king of the Assyrian Empire in the seventh century BCE, the son of Sennacherib and father of Ashurbanipal. He rebuilt Babylon and in 671 BCE invaded Egypt, driving out the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa and capturing Memphis, a defeat that began the Kushite Empire's…

eshnunna.s: Eshnunna was an ancient city-state in the Diyala valley, east of the Tigris, known for its law code. It was a rival of Babylon and was finally destroyed by Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire around 1755 BCE.

esigie.s: Esigie was an Oba of Benin who ruled during 1504–1550. He defeated the Igala and enlarged the Benin Empire, developed relations with the Portuguese, including trade and Christian missions, and his mother Idia became the first Iyoba (queen mother).

eso.s: The Eso were an elite corps of cavalry commanders in the Oyo Empire, traditionally numbering seventy, serving as the Alaafin's personal military instrument. They formed the organisational core of Oyo's cavalry army, which was central to the empire's expansion.

estado-da-india.s: The Estado da Índia was the Portuguese administration of its possessions in Asia and East Africa, headed by a viceroy or governor based at Goa from 1530. It coordinated the Portuguese Empire's network of fortified trading posts, and its intervention in the Horn of Africa,…

estado-novo-portugal.s: The Estado Novo ('New State') was the authoritarian regime that ruled Portugal from 1933 to 1974, led for most of that time by António de Oliveira Salazar. It insisted on keeping the colonies of the Portuguese Empire and fought costly colonial wars in Africa, until the…

estonia.s: Estonia is a country on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea. Northern Estonia came under Swedish rule in 1561, making it one of the first Baltic provinces of the Swedish Empire.

ethiopia.s: Ethiopia is a country in the Horn of Africa with one of the longest continuous state traditions in the world. It was the home of the Aksumite Empire and its successor, the Ethiopian Empire, fought a long war with the Adal Sultanate, and defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896 before…

ethiopian-empire.s: The Ethiopian Empire was the Christian monarchy of the Ethiopian highlands that lasted from the restoration of the Solomonic dynasty in 1270 until the deposition of Haile Selassie in 1974. It survived the Adal invasion in the sixteenth century, defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896…

ethiopian-highlands.s: The Ethiopian highlands are a large mountainous plateau in the Horn of Africa. Their fertile land and natural defences made them the heartland of the Aksumite Empire and its Christian successors, and their invasion by the Adal Sultanate in the sixteenth century came close to…

ethiopian-orthodox-church.s: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is the ancient Christian church of Ethiopia, belonging to the Oriental Orthodox communion. It was founded after the conversion of the Aksumite Empire under King Ezana in the fourth century and became a pillar of the Ethiopian Empire,…

ethiopian-adal-war.s: The Ethiopian–Adal War was a conflict fought in 1527–1543 between the Adal Sultanate, led by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, and the Christian Ethiopian Empire. Adal forces overran most of the highlands, but Portuguese intervention and Ahmad's death at the Battle of Wayna Daga in…

ethnic-hierarchy-and-discrimination.s: Ethnic hierarchy and discrimination refers to the formal or informal ranking of subjects by ethnicity or origin, which alienated large parts of an empire's population. The Yuan Dynasty divided its subjects into ranked classes with Chinese at the bottom, the Umayyad Caliphate…

ethnological-museum-berlin.s: The Ethnological Museum of Berlin is one of the largest museums of non-European art and cultures. It holds a major collection of Benin Bronzes looted from the Benin Empire by the British in 1897, and it has been a significant participant in the debate over restitution of these…

euclid.s: Euclid was a Greek mathematician of Alexandria, active around 300 BCE, whose Elements became the foundational textbook of geometry. His work was translated into Arabic during the translation movement of the Abbasid Caliphate, preserving and transmitting it to later Islamic and…

eumenes-ii.s: Eumenes II was king of Pergamon in the early second century BCE and an ally of Rome. His cavalry supported the Roman army at the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE, which inflicted a heavy defeat on the Seleucid Empire, and Pergamon received much of Seleucid Asia Minor afterwards.

eunuch.s: A eunuch is a castrated man, and in many courts eunuchs served as palace officials, guards of the royal household and administrators. Being unable to found dynasties, they were often trusted by rulers.

euphrates.s: The Euphrates is one of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, flowing from Anatolia through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Its waters supported the irrigation agriculture of the Akkadian Empire, the Neo-Sumerian Empire, the Babylonian Empire and the Chaldean Empire, and it…

eurasia.s: Eurasia is the combined landmass of Europe and Asia. Its steppe belt and trade routes linked empires across vast distances, enabling the expansion of nomadic powers such as the Xiongnu Empire and the Mongol Empire, and the exchange of goods and ideas through empires such as…

europe.s: Europe is the western part of the Eurasian landmass. It was the home of empires such as the Roman, Carolingian, Holy Roman and Austro-Hungarian, and from the fifteenth century European states built overseas empires that reached the Americas, Africa and Asia.

european-colonial-expansion.s: European colonial expansion describes the growth of European empires overseas from the fifteenth to the twentieth century, through trade, conquest and settlement. It undermined or destroyed many states, as in the British conquest of the Mughal Empire and Maratha Empire, French…

european-union.s: The European Union is a political and economic union of European states, developed from the European communities founded in the 1950s. Charlemagne and the Carolingian Empire, which united much of western Europe, are often invoked as symbolic forerunners of European unity in…

eusebio-de-queiros-law.s: The Eusébio de Queirós Law was a Brazilian law of 1850, named after the minister of justice who sponsored it, which effectively ended the transatlantic slave trade to the Brazilian Empire. Passed under heavy British pressure, it was an important step on the road towards the…

evian-accords.s: The Évian Accords were the agreements signed in 1962 between France and the Algerian National Liberation Front, ending the Algerian War. They led to Algeria's independence that year and marked one of the final chapters in the dismantling of the French Empire.

ewedo.s: Ewedo was an Oba of Benin who ruled c. 1260–1274.

eweka-i.s: Eweka I is the legendary first Oba of Benin, traditionally installed around 1180 CE after the Ogiso dynasty lost legitimacy. Tradition links him to Ife through his father Oranmiyan.

ewuakpe.s: Ewuakpe was an Oba of Benin whose reign, c. 1700–1712, saw a civil war that brought the Benin Empire close to collapse.

ewuare-the-great.s: Ewuare the Great was an Oba of Benin (r. 1440–1473) who transformed the kingdom into an empire.

execution-of-the-mongol-envoys-1218.s: The execution of the Mongol envoys in 1218 followed the massacre of a Mongol-sponsored trade caravan at Otrar. When Genghis Khan sent envoys to demand redress, Shah Muhammad II of the Khwarazmian Empire had them killed or humiliated.

expressionism.s: Expressionism was a modernist movement in art, literature and music in the early twentieth century that sought to express emotional experience rather than physical reality. In Vienna it flourished in the work of painters such as Egon Schiele and Oskar Kokoschka, forming part…

expulsion-of-the-jews-from-spain.n: Expulsion of the Jews from Spain
expulsion-of-the-jews-from-spain.s: The expulsion of the Jews from Spain was ordered by Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492, forcing Jews to convert or leave. Many of the exiles found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, where they settled in cities such as Istanbul and Thessaloniki and contributed to commerce, medicine and…

extraterritoriality.s: Extraterritoriality is the exemption of foreigners from the jurisdiction of local courts, so that they are tried under their own country's law. Imposed on the Qing Empire by the unequal treaties after the Opium Wars, it became a symbol of foreign encroachment on Chinese…

extremadura.s: Extremadura is a region of western Spain bordering Portugal. After the Almohad victory at Alarcos in 1195, Almohad Caliphate forces devastated Extremadura and neighbouring regions, raiding deep into Christian territory.

eyes-and-ears-of-the-king.n: Eyes and Ears of the King
eyes-and-ears-of-the-king.s: The 'Eyes and Ears of the King' were officials of the Achaemenid Empire who, according to Greek sources, acted as royal inspectors and informants. They reported to the king on the conduct of satraps and the state of the provinces, serving as a check on provincial power.

ezana.s: Ezana was a king of Aksum who reigned c. 325–340 CE.

ezana-stone.s: The Ezana Stone is an inscribed stela at Aksum recording the deeds of King Ezana in the fourth century CE. Written in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek, it commemorates his military campaigns and reflects his conversion to Christianity.
